{{Short description|Unique strong solution of a stochastic differential equation}}
In [[stochastic calculus]], the '''Doléans-Dade exponential''' or '''stochastic exponential''' of a [[semimartingale]] ''X'' is the unique strong solution of the [[stochastic differential equation]] <math display="block">dY_t = Y_{t-}\,dX_t,\quad\quad Y_0=1,</math>where <math>Y_{-}</math> denotes the process of left limits, i.e., <math>Y_{t-}=\lim_{s\uparrow t}Y_s</math>.

The concept is named after [[Catherine Doléans-Dade]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Doléans-Dade|first=C.|date=1970|title=Quelques applications de la formule de changement de variables pour les semimartingales|journal=Zeitschrift für Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und Verwandte Gebiete |trans-journal=Probability Theory and Related Fields|language=fr|volume=16|issue=3|pages=181–194|doi=10.1007/BF00534595|s2cid=118181229 |issn=0044-3719|doi-access=free}}</ref>  The stochastic exponential plays an important role in the formulation of [[Girsanov theorem|Girsanov's theorem]] and arises naturally in all applications where relative changes are important since <math>X</math> measures the cumulative percentage change in <math>Y</math>.

== Notation and terminology ==
Process <math>Y</math> obtained above is commonly denoted by <math>\mathcal{E}(X)</math>. The terminology "stochastic exponential" arises from the similarity of <math>\mathcal{E}(X)=Y</math> to the natural exponential of <math>X</math>: If ''X'' is [[Absolute continuity|absolutely continuous]] with respect to time, then ''Y'' solves, path-by-path, the differential equation <math>dY_t/\mathrm{d}t = Y_tdX_t/dt</math>, whose solution is <math>Y=\exp(X-X_0)</math>.

== General formula and special cases ==

* Without any assumptions on the semimartingale <math>X</math>, one has <math display="block">\mathcal{E}(X)_t = \exp\Bigl(X_t-X_0-\frac12[X]^c_t\Bigr)\prod_{s\le t}(1+\Delta X_s) \exp (-\Delta X_s),\qquad t\ge0,</math>where <math>[X]^c</math> is the continuous part of quadratic variation of <math>X</math> and the product extends over the (countably many) jumps of ''X'' up to time ''t''.
* If <math>X</math> is continuous, then <math display="block">\mathcal{E}(X) = \exp\Bigl(X-X_0-\frac12[X]\Bigr).</math>In particular, if <math>X</math> is a [[Wiener process|Brownian motion]], then the Doléans-Dade exponential is a [[geometric Brownian motion]]. 
* If <math>X</math> is continuous and of finite variation, then <math display="block">\mathcal{E}(X)=\exp(X-X_0).</math>Here <math>X</math> need not be differentiable with respect to time; for example, <math>X</math> can be the [[Cantor function]].

== Properties ==

* A stochastic exponential cannot go to zero continuously; it can only jump to zero. Hence, the stochastic exponential of a continuous semimartingale is always strictly positive.
* Once <math>\mathcal{E}(X)</math> has jumped to zero, it is absorbed in zero. The first time it jumps to zero is precisely the first time when <math>\Delta X=-1</math>. 
*Unlike the natural exponential <math>\exp(X_t)</math>, which depends only of the value of <math>X</math> at time <math>t</math>, the stochastic exponential <math>\mathcal{E}(X)_t</math> depends not only on <math>X_t</math> but on the whole history of <math>X</math> in the time interval <math>[0,t]</math>. For this reason one must write <math>\mathcal{E}(X)_t</math> and not <math>\mathcal{E}(X_t)</math>.
* Natural exponential of a semimartingale can always be written as a stochastic exponential of another semimartingale but not the other way around.
* Stochastic exponential of a local martingale is again a local martingale.
* All the formulae and properties above apply also to stochastic exponential of a [[Complex number|complex]]-valued <math>X</math>. This has application in the theory of conformal martingales and in the calculation of characteristic functions.

== Useful identities ==
Yor's formula:<ref>{{Citation|last=Yor|first=Marc|chapter=Sur les integrales stochastiques optionnelles et une suite remarquable de formules exponentielles |title=Séminaire de Probabilités X Université de Strasbourg |date=1976|chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/bfb0101123|series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics |volume=511 |pages=481–500|place=Berlin, Heidelberg|publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg|doi=10.1007/bfb0101123 |isbn=978-3-540-07681-0 |s2cid=118228097 |url=http://www.numdam.org/item/SPS_1976__10__481_0/ |access-date=2021-12-14|url-access=subscription}}</ref> for any two semimartingales <math>U</math> and <math>V</math> one has <math display="block">\mathcal{E}(U)\mathcal{E}(V) = \mathcal{E}(U+V+[U,V])</math>

== Applications ==

* The stochastic exponential of a local martingale appears  in the statement of [[Girsanov theorem]]. Criteria to ensure that the stochastic exponential <math>\mathcal{E}(X)</math> of a continuous local martingale <math>X</math> is a [[martingale (probability theory)|martingale]] are given by [[Kazamaki's condition]], [[Novikov's condition]], and [[Beneš's condition]].

== Derivation of the explicit formula for continuous semimartingales ==
For any continuous semimartingale ''X'', take for granted that <math>Y</math> is continuous and strictly positive. Then applying [[Itō's lemma|Itō's formula]] with  {{nowrap|''ƒ''(''Y'') {{=}} log(''Y'')}} gives

:<math>
\begin{align}
\log(Y_t)-\log(Y_0) &= \int_0^t\frac{1}{Y_u}\,dY_u -\int_0^t\frac{1}{2Y_u^2}\,d[Y]_u
= X_t-X_0 - \frac{1}{2}[X]_t.
\end{align}
</math>

Exponentiating with <math>
Y_0=1
</math> gives the solution

:<math>Y_t = \exp\Bigl(X_t-X_0-\frac12[X]_t\Bigr),\qquad t\ge0.</math>

This differs from what might be expected by comparison with the case where ''X'' has finite variation due to the existence of the [[quadratic variation]] term  <nowiki>[</nowiki>''X''<nowiki>]</nowiki> in the solution.
